e.t: This word means “be watchful” or “to keep awake.” It describes staying alert rather than becoming spiritually or mentally careless. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, expressing a continuing call to remain attentive and ready. Its ordinary sense is active vigilance: a person does not drift into inattention but stays awake and watchful. The surrounding passage determines what the person is to watch for or remain ready to do.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to send” or “to send back.” It describes the act of dispatching a person or directing someone onward, and it can also indicate returning someone to a previous authority or place. The word occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke, Acts, and Philemon. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who is being sent and where the surrounding passage directs that person.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to throw away.” It describes the action of casting something off or setting it aside rather than keeping it. As a verb, it focuses on the act of removing or discarding something. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 10:50 and Hebrews 10:35. The surrounding wording determines what is being thrown away in each passage, but the central idea remains an active separation from something previously held or possessed.

This word means “idle,” describing someone or something not actively engaged in useful work or activity. It can refer to people who are simply unoccupied, and it can also describe speech or faith that lacks meaningful action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times across seven verses, including passages in Matthew, 1 Timothy, Titus, James, and 2 Peter. Its central idea is not merely resting, but being inactive or unproductive when activity or useful results are expected.

e.t: This word means “to catch” or “to seize”—to take hold of someone or something, sometimes suddenly or forcefully. It can describe physically taking a person, animal, or object, or claiming control of something that is being taken away. The word appears 14 times in the Greek New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being caught or seized and the surrounding sentence.

This word describes an “expert builder” or “master-builder”—a person responsible for skilled, foundational construction. It presents building as work requiring knowledge, care, and leadership rather than merely physical labor. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Corinthians 3:10, and its ordinary sense is best understood as a highly skilled builder who establishes or directs the work. The surrounding verse context is needed to explain how this image functions there.

e.t: This Greek verb means “to consider” or “to fix one’s eyes,” describing deliberate attention directed toward something. It points to more than briefly noticing; it expresses turning the mind or gaze toward a chosen object. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Philippians 2:23 and Hebrews 12:2. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains focused consideration or attentive looking.

Blastus is a personal name, referring to a man identified by that name. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 12:20. Because it functions as a name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who a person is, not what quality, action, or condition he represents. The name is rendered consistently as “Blastus.”

e.t: This word means “fifteen,” the number that comes after fourteen and before sixteen. It is a number word used to state an exact count, amount, or measurement rather than to describe a person, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in John, Acts, and Galatians. Its precise significance in any particular sentence comes from the object or measurement being counted there.

e.t: This word means “to make a covenant”—to establish a binding agreement or promised relationship. It is used as an action word, emphasizing the making or establishing of the covenant rather than merely referring to one already in place. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times across six verses, especially in Hebrews, where it is associated with God’s covenant promises and their establishment. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word describes a persecutor—a person who actively pursues, harasses, or opposes others. It presents persecution as an identifying role, not merely a passing action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 1:13, and is rendered “persecutor.” The word’s central meaning is therefore a person engaged in hostile pursuit or oppression of others. The surrounding verse supplies the specific circumstances and personal significance of that description.

This word refers to Gentiles—the nations or peoples viewed as distinct from Israel. It can describe non-Israelite people collectively, whether they are discussed as nations, communities, or the wider peoples of the world. In the Greek New Testament it appears 162 times, so it is a broad and recurring term rather than a title for one particular group. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding wording.

e.t: This word means “to rush in” or “to rush into,” describing sudden, energetic movement into a place or situation. It functions as an action word, emphasizing the force or urgency of entering rather than a quiet or gradual arrival. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 16:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains an abrupt movement inward. The word therefore portrays someone entering quickly and decisively.

e.t: This word means “to escape”—to get away from danger, judgment, confinement, or an approaching circumstance. It describes the act of successfully avoiding or departing from something rather than facing its full effect. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, including passages about escaping danger, punishment, or coming events. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains removal from a threatening or difficult situation.

Emmaus is the name of a place. In the Greek New Testament, this word refers to Emmaus and appears once, in Luke 24:13. Because it is a place name rather than a descriptive word, its basic meaning is the location itself, not an action, quality, or spiritual condition. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what happens there, but the word’s direct reference is simply the place called Emmaus.

This Greek New Testament word refers to a thought or reflection—the mental consideration present within a person. It describes what someone is thinking or contemplating. The word occurs four times in the New Testament corpus, appearing twice in Matthew and once each in Acts and Hebrews. Its basic meaning centers on the inner activity of thought, whether that thought is considered privately or recognized as part of a person’s reasoning. The surrounding verse determines the specific force of the thought in each occurrence.

e.t: This word means “sixty,” the number that comes after fifty-nine and before sixty-one. It is a number word used to state an amount or count. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, including passages that describe differing yields from seed, a distance traveled, an age requirement, and numerical details in Revelation. Its meaning remains straightforward wherever it appears, while the surrounding sentence determines what is being counted or measured.

This word means “in the act” or “in the very act,” describing someone caught while the action is actually happening. It is more specific than a general accusation: it points to the deed being witnessed at the moment of its occurrence. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, in John 8:4. The surrounding verse supplies the particular action meant there, while the word itself emphasizes immediate discovery.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to dwell” or “to rest upon,” describing the act of settling or remaining upon something. Its central idea is an abiding presence rather than a brief contact. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:9. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning concerns dwelling or resting upon something.

This Greek New Testament word marks a limit or endpoint, meaning “until” or “up to”; it can also express “even” in some sentences. It commonly shows how long something continues or the point reached by an action, time, or sequence. The word appears 146 times in the Greek New Testament, across 137 verses, so its precise force depends on what it connects in each sentence. Its central idea remains a boundary, whether temporal or extending to a stated point.

e.t: This word means “to nurse a baby” or “to suckle.” It describes feeding an infant at the breast and can refer to a nursing mother or to babies who depend on nursing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its plain sense remains connected with infancy, motherhood, and the physical care required by a child who is still nursing. The surrounding verse determines whether the word highlights the nursing child, the mother, or the hardship associated with caring for infants.

The word means “curtain”: a hanging that covers or divides a space. It occurs six times in the Greek New Testament, with three occurrences in Hebrews. The same central idea applies across its uses, whether the word refers to a physical hanging or is used in discussing access and separation. The precise force in each verse comes from its surrounding passage, but the basic meaning remains a curtain or dividing covering.

e.t: This word means “to devour,” “to eat up,” or “devoured.” It describes consuming something completely or forcefully, whether the sentence presents the action as ongoing or already completed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 14 times, so its central idea remains consistent across several passages. The surrounding verse determines what is being consumed and whether the word is used literally or figuratively; the word itself emphasizes thorough, consuming action rather than a small or casual act of eating.

This word means “sleep,” referring to the state of resting or being asleep. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in John 11:13, so its normal meaning is established by this single occurrence and its explicit lexical sense. The word itself names sleep rather than explaining the surrounding event or adding a separate spiritual meaning. The precise force of its use in John depends on the verse and its surrounding context.

e.t: This word means “to arrange” or “to make beautiful.” It describes putting something in order or adorning it so that it appears prepared, orderly, or attractive. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 10 times and can describe arranging a house, preparing lamps, beautifying buildings, or adorning oneself. Its central idea is purposeful order and beauty rather than mere existence or appearance.

This word means “hunger,” referring to the condition of lacking enough food and the bodily need that results. In the Greek New Testament, it can describe personal deprivation as well as famine affecting a wider population. It appears 12 times across 12 verses, including passages that speak of hunger among distressing events and a person experiencing severe need. Its basic sense remains straightforward: an absence of food that produces hunger, whether suffered by an individual or experienced broadly as famine.

This word describes someone who is “hardly able to talk” or “hardly talking.” It refers to severely limited speech, emphasizing difficulty in expressing words aloud rather than ordinary silence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 7:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to a person whose ability to speak is greatly impaired.

This word means “lawgiver”: a person who gives, establishes, or authoritatively sets a law. It is a noun naming the one responsible for law, rather than the law itself or someone merely obeying it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 4:12. The word therefore points to the authority behind a law, while the surrounding verse is needed to show how James applies that title.

This word means “a fathom,” a unit used to measure depth. It describes a distance downward or the depth of water rather than an object, person, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both within one verse in Acts.27.28. The plural rendering “fathoms” reflects the measurement being counted. Its basic meaning is therefore a practical measurement of depth; the surrounding verse supplies the particular depth being measured.

This word describes ongoing friction, dispute, or contention between people. It can point to a persistent atmosphere of quarrels rather than a single disagreement, capturing the idea of “constant friction” and “contention.” In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 6:5. The surrounding verse context is needed to explain how this word functions in that specific passage, but its central meaning is continued strife or argumentative conflict.

This word refers to a barracks or military camp—a place where soldiers are stationed. It can describe an organized military enclosure rather than merely an open field or temporary gathering place. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, including several passages in Acts involving Roman soldiers and their quarters, and later uses referring to a camp. Its basic sense remains a designated place occupied or defended by military forces.

This word means “poor,” describing a person who has very little material wealth. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, so its normal meaning is represented by a single passage rather than a broad range of uses. In Luke 21:2, it identifies the condition of the person being described, but the precise force of the word in that verse belongs to the surrounding verse and passage. Its central sense is straightforward: lacking financial resources.

Abundance means a plentiful or overflowing amount—more than what is merely sufficient. In the Greek New Testament, this word expresses an excess or rich supply, whether referring to what is received, possessed, or present. It occurs four times in the New Testament. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what the surrounding sentence says is abundant, but the central idea remains fullness beyond ordinary measure.

This word means greediness: an improper desire to have more. It describes a self-seeking appetite for possessions or advantage rather than a contented and generous disposition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, including passages that place it among serious sinful attitudes and behaviors. Its use as a noun identifies greediness as a settled quality or governing desire, not merely a single moment of wanting something. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word means “how often!”. It asks about the frequency of an action—how many times something happens or should happen. As a question, it seeks a number or repeated pattern rather than describing the action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Matthew and Luke, showing its use in questions about repeated actions. Its precise force in any particular sentence comes from the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains clear: asking how many times or how often. e.t: This word means “follow” or “to follow.” It describes moving after someone or proceeding in the same direction, and it can also express continuing in an established way. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in Acts, Romans, Galatians, and Philippians. Its basic sense is straightforward: to follow a person, course, or standard rather than turn aside from it. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This word means “to be joined together” or “to join.” It describes parts being brought together into a connected whole rather than remaining separate. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Ephesians, where its basic idea concerns unity and connectedness. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central meaning remains the act of joining parts together so they function as one. This is a verb expressing connection, fitting together, or being united.

This word means “tax collector,” referring to a person who collected taxes. In the Greek New Testament, it is used as a title for such a person rather than as a general word for money, payment, or taxation. The word occurs 21 times across 20 verses, appearing in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its use in several Gospel passages shows that tax collectors are spoken of as a recognizable group of people. The surrounding passage determines the particular point being made whenever the word appears.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to exalt” or “to exalt to the highest place.” It describes raising someone to the highest position of honor or status. As a verb, it expresses the action of lifting someone up in rank or distinction. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 2:9. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on supreme elevation and honor.

This word means “murder,” referring to the unlawful killing of another person. It functions as a noun, naming the act or crime rather than describing the person who commits it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times across nine verses, including passages that speak of murder as a serious evil and of people accused or imprisoned for it. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “worse” or “worse than,” describing something that is more harmful, undesirable, or serious in comparison with something else. It is a comparative word, so its meaning normally depends on the thing being contrasted, whether that contrast is stated directly or understood from the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times, from Matthew through 2 Peter. Its central idea remains a decline from a previous or competing condition to one that is worse.

This word means “as” or “just as,” linking one statement with another by showing correspondence or comparison. It functions as a connecting word rather than naming a person, object, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Hebrews 5:4. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being compared, but the word itself signals that the following statement is to be understood in relation to something already stated.
